text: After I had driven about the suburbs in my carriage for several days, I learned that the landlord had called the police and that Bartleby had been removed, as a vagrant, to the Tombs, the city prison. <break time="0.8s" /> When I went to see him, I found him standing all alone in the quietest of the yards, his face toward a high wall. <break time="0.8s" /> I know you, he said without looking round, and I want nothing to say to you, and when I assured him that this was not so sad a place, he answered, I know where I am. <break time="0.8s" /> I paid the prison cook to give him the best dinner he could find, but Bartleby, turning again toward the wall, only said that he preferred not to dine that day, for it would disagree with him. <break time="0.8s" /> A few days later, I found him lying strangely huddled at the base of the wall, his knees drawn up and his head touching the cold stones, and I knew that he had quietly passed away. <break time="0.8s" /> He is asleep, is he not, asked the cook, and I murmured, With kings and counselors, recalling the ancient words of Job about those who rest in peace. <break time="0.8s" /> Months afterward I heard a rumor, whose truth I cannot confirm, that Bartleby had once been a clerk in the Dead Letter Office at Washington, from which he had been suddenly removed by a change in the administration. <break time="0.8s" /> On errands of life these letters speed to death, carrying a ring for a finger now in the grave or a pardon for one who died despairing, and I can only sigh, Ah Bartleby, Ah humanity.
